_status: DRAFT v3 by Claude, Oct 15 2026. Not reviewed by a clinician. Languages: en (default), ur (Urdu script), ur-roman (Roman Urdu with natural English code-switching) in exercises_i18n.json, all pending native review. Wording is Claude's adaptation; structure follows the cited sources. Every number is listed in NUMBERS with its source or marked as an engineering default.
_urdu: Drafted by Claude (exercises_i18n.json), pending native review. Reviewer can align terms with WHO's official Urdu PM+ and the Urdu Thinking Healthy Programme.
_safety_rules: No exercise is ever offered at CRITICAL. PM+ 'was not developed for use with ... a plan to end one's life in the near future', and THP excludes imminent suicide risk: exercises are never a substitute for the crisis path.
At HIGH, only exercises with crisis_modal_ok=true may appear, below the helplines, never auto-started (Decision 2, pending Ahmad).
Every free-text answer the user types inside an exercise is still a conversational turn: it passes through the per-turn crisis check, and HIGH/CRITICAL interrupts the exercise (policy.py R1).
Breathing: no breath holds and no 'deep breaths'. WHO DWM: if breathing makes you dizzy, 'DO NOT take deep breaths'.
Eyes-open by default; no long eyes-closed or body-scan practices (meditation-related adverse experiences are documented: Lindahl et al. 2017, PLOS ONE).
Thought and problem exercises stop and offer help if the topic is self-harm, harming others, abuse or danger; they are not for working on trauma memories.

offer.text: Would you like to try a short breathing exercise with me? You can choose 1 minute or 5 minutes.
offer.what_is_it: You breathe a little more slowly than usual, about six breaths a minute, following a circle on the screen. Slow breathing is linked with feeling calmer and less anxious. You can stop at any time.

decline_followup.text: That's okay. Is it the breathing itself, or just not the right moment?

Breathing isn't for me.text: Fair enough. Some people find it easier to notice what's around them instead. Would you like to try one of these?

Not the right moment.text: No problem. If you have about 30 seconds, there's a very short one you can do anywhere. Or we can leave it for later.

safety_note: Breathe at a pace that feels okay for you. You can stop at any time. If you feel dizzy or more uneasy, stop and breathe normally.

post_check.text: How is your mood right now?
post_check.on_low: Thanks for telling me. Do you want to talk about what's going on?
post_check.save_go_to: Save this as my go-to exercise

exercises.title: Slow breathing
exercises.source: Pace: resonance breathing at ~6 breaths/min (Lehrer & Gevirtz 2014) and slow breathing <10/min (Zaccaro et al. 2018). Session: 5 min/day (Balban et al. 2023). Structure adapted from WHO PM+ 'Managing stress' and WHO DWM grounding.
exercises.what_is_it: Breathe in gently, then breathe out a little longer, about six breaths a minute, following a circle.
exercises.intro: Let's slow the breath down together. Follow the circle: breathe in as it grows, and out as it shrinks.
cautions: Stop and breathe normally if dizzy.
exercises.outro: Well done. Take a moment before you carry on.
exercises.crisis_modal_note: Allowed below the helplines at HIGH (Ahmad, Oct 15: prefer the wider pool). Never at CRITICAL.

exercises.title: Cyclic sighing
exercises.source: Balban et al. 2023, Cell Reports Medicine (RCT, n=108): 5 minutes/day of cyclic sighing gave the largest daily improvement in positive mood of the techniques tested, and reduced anxiety.
exercises.crisis_modal_note: Not in the crisis modal: the double inhale is more effortful than plain slow breathing.
exercises.what_is_it: Two breaths in through the nose (a normal one, then a short top-up), then a long, slow breath out through the mouth. A study found five minutes a day of this lifted mood.
exercises.intro: Breathe in through your nose, add a short second sip of air, then let it all out slowly through your mouth.

phases.label: Breathe out slowly through your mouth

cautions: Keep the top-up small and gentle.
Stop and breathe normally if dizzy.
exercises.outro: Nicely done. Notice how your body feels now.

exercises.title: Notice, slow down, refocus
exercises.source: Adapted from WHO 'Doing What Matters in Times of Stress' (2020), skill 1: grounding.
exercises.crisis_modal_note: Allowed below the helplines at HIGH; never auto-started; never at CRITICAL. DWM describes grounding as keeping you safe 'until the storm passes'.
exercises.what_is_it: A two-minute way to steady yourself when feelings are strong: notice what's happening, slow down, and bring your attention back to where you are.
exercises.intro: When feelings are strong, it can help to steady yourself first. Take each step at your own pace and tap Next when you're ready.
steps: Notice what you're feeling and thinking right now. You don't have to change it, just notice it.
Slow down. Breathe out slowly, gently stretch your arms or shoulders, and press your feet into the floor.
Look around and name a few things you can see.
Listen for a few things you can hear.
Notice something you can touch: the chair, your clothes, the phone in your hand.
Now bring your attention back to what you were doing and who is around you.
exercises.outro: This doesn't make the feelings disappear, but it can help you stay steady until they ease.

exercises.title: 5-4-3-2-1 senses
exercises.source: Common counting variant of the 'refocus' step in WHO DWM grounding (which names five things you can see and three or four you can hear). The 5-4-3-2-1 counting itself is not from DWM.
exercises.what_is_it: A short exercise that uses your five senses to bring your attention back to the room you're in.
exercises.intro: Let's bring your attention to what's around you. Take each step at your own pace and tap Next when you're ready.
steps: Look around and notice 5 things you can see.
Notice 4 things you can feel, like your feet on the floor or the chair under you.
Listen for 3 things you can hear.
Notice 2 things you can smell, or two smells you like.
Notice 1 thing you can taste, or take a sip of water.
exercises.outro: Nice work. Notice how you feel right now.

exercises.title: Unhooking from a thought
exercises.source: Adapted from WHO DWM (2020), skill 2: unhooking (notice, name, refocus).
exercises.what_is_it: A 30-second skill for when a worrying thought keeps pulling you away: notice it, give it a name, and come back to what you're doing.
exercises.intro: Sometimes a thought grabs hold and drags our attention away. Here's a quick way to unhook.
steps: Notice: is a thought or feeling pulling your attention away right now?
Name it quietly to yourself, for example: 'I'm noticing the thought that I'm not good enough' or 'I'm noticing a knot in my stomach.'
Refocus: bring your attention back to what you're doing, or to this conversation, and give it your full attention.
exercises.outro: Thoughts may come back, and that's normal. Each time, you can notice, name and refocus again.

exercises.title: Being kind to yourself
exercises.source: Adapted from WHO DWM (2020), skill 4: being kind.
exercises.what_is_it: A short exercise for when you're being hard on yourself: notice the unkind thoughts and try talking to yourself the way you'd talk to a friend.
exercises.intro: We're often much harsher with ourselves than with anyone else. Let's try something different for a minute.
steps: Notice any unkind thoughts you've been having about yourself. Unkind thoughts are very common, and that's okay.
Name them: 'I'm noticing I'm being hard on myself.'
Ask: what would I say to a close friend who felt this way?
Try saying something like that to yourself, quietly or in your head.
If it feels okay, place a hand where you feel the hurt, maybe your chest, and breathe slowly and warmly towards it.
exercises.outro: Being kind to yourself is a skill. It can feel strange at first, and it gets easier with practice.

exercises.title: Making room for a feeling
exercises.source: Adapted from WHO DWM (2020), skill 5: making room.
exercises.why_not_offered: It asks the user to stay with a painful feeling, which can intensify it; Claude's judgement is that it should only be chosen by the user or used inside the CBT module, never auto-offered.
exercises.what_is_it: An exercise for a painful feeling that won't go away: instead of fighting it, you look at it with curiosity and let it be there for a moment.
exercises.intro: Feelings are a bit like the weather: they come and they go. Let's try making a little room for one, eyes open, at your own pace. You can stop at any point.
steps: Notice a feeling that's here right now, and name it: 'Here is sadness' or 'Here is worry.'
Get curious: where do you feel it in your body? If it had a size, shape or colour, what would it be?
Breathe slowly in and around it. You don't have to like it, just let it be there for a moment.
Now widen your attention back out: notice the room around you and what you were doing.
exercises.stop_if: If the feeling gets much stronger or overwhelming, stop and switch to 'Notice, slow down, refocus'.
exercises.outro: You let the feeling be there without being pushed around by it. That's a real skill.

exercises.title: Checking an unhelpful thought
exercises.source: Core CBT skill (identifying and challenging unhelpful thoughts), as used in the WHO Thinking Healthy Programme (CBT-based, trialled in rural Pakistan, Urdu translation available). Loneliness focus: Masi et al. (2011) found interventions targeting maladaptive social cognition were the most effective loneliness interventions. The Socratic prompts are Claude's wording.
exercises.licence: Claude's wording; THP licence not confirmed
exercises.what_is_it: A step-by-step way to look at a thought that's bringing you down, check how true it really is, and find a fairer way to see things. It's one of the main tools in CBT.
exercises.intro: Let's look at one thought together. I'll ask a few questions; answer in your own words, and you can stop at any time.
examples_for_loneliness: Nobody wants to talk to me.
If I message them, I'll just be bothering them.
Everyone else has friends except me.

prompts.ask: What's the thought that's bothering you? Try to write it as a sentence.
How strongly do you believe it right now, from 0 to 100?
What makes you think this thought is true?
Is there anything that doesn't quite fit with it, even something small?
If a close friend had this thought about themselves, what would you say to them?
Putting that together, is there a fairer or kinder way to say the thought?
How strongly do you believe the original thought now, from 0 to 100?

exercises.reflection: Thoughts aren't facts. Even a small shift in how strongly you believe a thought can make a difference.
exercises.stop_if: If the thought is about hurting yourself or someone else, the exercise stops and the crisis path takes over. Not for working through traumatic memories.
exercises.save: Save this so you can look back at it later

exercises.title: One small thing today
exercises.source: Adapted from WHO PM+ (2018) strategy 'Get going, keep doing' (behavioural activation: increasing activity to improve mood); THP also uses behavioural activation. Step wording and the activity examples are Claude's.
exercises.what_is_it: When we feel low, we tend to do less, and doing less makes us feel lower. This breaks the cycle with one small, doable activity.
exercises.intro: Let's pick one small thing you could do today or tomorrow, something pleasant or something useful.
activity_examples: Have chai with someone at home
Listen to a song you like
Sit in the sun for a few minutes
Play a sport or a game for a bit
Something that feels meaningful to you

prompts.ask: What's one small thing you could do? Pick from the list or write your own.
When could you do it? Be as specific as you can.
How confident are you that you'll do it, from 0 (not at all) to 10 (completely)?

if_commitment_below.say: Let's make it a bit smaller so it feels doable. What's a shorter or simpler version?
if_commitment_below.source: Brief Action Planning: below 7, problem-solve the plan.

exercises.follow_up: Asked at the next check-in (UX Flow 2). If it didn't happen, gently explore what got in the way and make the task smaller. Never penalised (UX Flows 2 and 12).

exercises.title: Working through a problem
exercises.source: Adapted from WHO PM+ (2018) strategy 'Managing problems' (listing possible solutions and choosing the most helpful); structured problem-solving is also part of THP. Step wording is Claude's.
exercises.what_is_it: A step-by-step way to break a practical problem into pieces, think of options, and choose a first step.
exercises.intro: Let's take one problem and break it down. We'll go step by step.

prompts.ask: What's one problem that's on your mind? A practical one works best.
Is any part of this something you can change, even a little?
prompts.if_no: Some problems can't be changed right now. In that case, looking after how you cope matters more. Would you like to try 'Making room for a feeling' or 'Being kind to yourself'?

prompts.ask: Let's list ideas, without judging them yet. What are some things you could do? Write as many as you like.
Which idea looks most helpful and doable?
What's the very first step, and when will you do it?
Is there anyone who could help with this?

exercises.stop_if: If the problem involves danger, abuse, or harming yourself or others, stop and show the help options instead of problem-solving.
exercises.follow_up: Review at the next check-in: what happened, and what's the next step?
exercises.save: Add the first step to my tasks

exercises.title: A step towards what matters
exercises.source: Adapted from WHO DWM (2020), skill 3: acting on values (choose values, pick one relationship, one small action this week).
exercises.what_is_it: Values are about the kind of person you want to be, like caring, honest or brave. This helps you choose one small action that fits them.
exercises.intro: Goals are what we want to get; values are the kind of person we want to be. Let's find one small step that fits yours.

prompts.ask: Which one or two of these matter most to you? Or write your own.
Think of one relationship that matters to you. Who is it?
What's one small thing you could do this week, in that relationship, that fits your values?

exercises.title: Who's in my corner?
exercises.source: Adapted from WHO PM+ (2018) strategy 'Strengthening social support' (support from trusted friends, family, co-workers or community organisations). Pairs with thought_check for loneliness thoughts (Masi et al. 2011). Prompts are Claude's wording.
exercises.what_is_it: A short exercise to notice who you could lean on, even a little, and pick one easy way to connect.
exercises.intro: When we feel alone, it's easy to forget the people who might be there for us. Let's take a gentle look.

prompts.ask: Who is someone you feel safe with, even if you haven't talked in a while? A friend, cousin, sibling, classmate, neighbour or teacher all count.
What's one easy way to connect with them? For example: send a short message, share something funny, or ask how they are.
Is there a group or place where you could be around people, like a class, a community or religious group, or a sports ground?
How uneasy would that step feel, from 0 (completely calm) to 100 (the most uneasy you can imagine)?
How confident are you that you'll take that step, from 0 (not at all) to 10 (completely)?

exercises.safety: Only people the user feels safe with. Never suggest contacting a specific person, and never push contact with anyone the user describes as hurtful or unsafe.
exercises.next: Can become the first step on the Social Ladder (UX Flow 11).

if_commitment_below.say: That's okay. What would make it easier, or is there a smaller first step, like just reading their last message?
if_commitment_below.source: Brief Action Planning: below 7, problem-solve the plan.

ladder_rules.if_gap_larger: split the step into smaller steps (UX Flow 11 'step-splitting')

considered_and_not_added.why: Breath holds can feel uncomfortable for anxious users, and WHO DWM warns against deep breaths when dizzy. Kept out of the default.

considered_and_not_added.what: Long eyes-closed meditation or body scans
considered_and_not_added.why: Meditation-related challenging experiences are documented (Lindahl et al. 2017). Not suitable unsupervised for a distressed audience.

considered_and_not_added.what: Imagery or working through traumatic memories

considered_and_not_added.why: Common, but not sourced in this session. Can be added after sourcing.

considered_and_not_added.what: Any exercise at CRITICAL, or as a replacement for helplines
considered_and_not_added.why: PM+ and THP both exclude people with a plan to end their life or at imminent suicide risk.

NUMBERS.source: Resonance breathing ~0.1 Hz = six breaths per minute (Lehrer & Gevirtz 2014, Frontiers in Psychology); slow breathing defined as <10 breaths/min with reduced anxiety and arousal (Zaccaro et al. 2018 systematic review).

An RCT comparing longer-exhale vs equal ratios found a small, non-significant extra benefit (d=0.2); 'breath ratios do not have a significant differential effect'. Kept because WHO DWM also says 'breathe out slowly'.

5 minutes daily of cyclic sighing improved mood and reduced anxiety over a month (Balban et al. 2023, Cell Reports Medicine RCT, n=108). The 1-minute option is a convenience choice with no specific source.

NUMBERS.value: 2 s in + 1 s top-up in, 6 s slow out (about 6-7 breaths/min)
NUMBERS.source: Pattern from Balban et al. 2023 (two inhales, long exhale). Second counts are Claude's estimate kept under 10 breaths/min (Zaccaro 2018).
Brief Action Planning (clinician technique): when confidence is below 7, use collaborative problem solving; people are more likely to succeed at 7 or more.

NUMBERS.what: Distress rating for Social Ladder steps
NUMBERS.value: SUDS 0-100; adjacent steps no more than 10 apart, else split
NUMBERS.source: Wolpe's Subjective Units of Disturbance scale (0-100); hierarchy items spaced 'no more than 5 to 10 SUDs' apart.
Standard CBT thought-record convention (Beck); not re-verified in this session.
No clinical source; simple scale chosen for a phone. Maps to the existing mood_rating field.
Morrison et al. 2017 (PLOS ONE): up to 3 notifications/day did not lower response rates; authors caution several per day may be unacceptable and exact thresholds are unknown.

NUMBERS.status: 24 h loosely sourced; 72 h engineering default
NUMBERS.source: A daily schedule had no response-rate penalty (Morrison et al. 2017).

NUMBERS.what: Smoothing and hysteresis (EWMA 0.3, disarm 0.30, min 3 turns), grounding cooldown 2 h
NUMBERS.source: No clinical source exists for these; they control how often the app interrupts, and are disclosed as tunable.
